utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, and rather briefly, just two quick questions. The first relating, Lieutenant-Colonel Fortin, to your testimony which for the record in this case appears at page 43, approximately -- beginning at about lines 7 and 8, and there you speak alternatively about mortars and heavy weapons and heavy mortars around the PTT building. And the question I'd like to ask you is: Could you clarify what weapons to your knowledge had the Bosnians placed around the PTT building at the time of the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I recall, they were 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, have you had some training in artillery, training and experience in artillery over the course of your military career, Lieutenant-Colonel Fortin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As an army officer, I got advanced training on the use of mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in common military speak, is an 82-millimetre mortar a heavy weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a light mortar, in all categories a mortar, but I believe for the purpose of an exclusion zone all indirect fire weapons were included as heavy weapons in the context of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your answers about the PTT building, you were offering assistance to the direct targeting of the PTT building. Now, I'd like your further assistance and your opinion, having been there at the time. In your opinion, were the Bosnian Serbs targeting those mortars or were they targeting the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, like I said, the Serbs were usually very accurate with their mortars. That day we received three rounds of mortars, two directly on the building and the other one in the parking lot. So the greatest distance between the two furthest apart of those three rounds was probably about 30 metres, which is quite accurate, and that's why I say they were directly targeting the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But where were the mortars placed in relation to the building? Were they directly behind it or to the side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian mortars were to the north of the building, a few hundred metres to the north of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From where the fire was coming, would that be in front or behind it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the fire was coming from Lukavica, but I'm not certain. So in this case they would have been behind the building, if the fire was coming from Lukavica, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were they immediately behind it, directly behind it, or -- or to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few hundred metres, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A few hundred metres behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One further question related to the incidents around that same time, the shelling of the TV building and the shelling of the PTT building, and for that purpose, I wonder if I could ask for a document to be shown on the screen. It's already in evidence and bears the number P18, please. Now, I see in front of me a Serbo-Croatian version and I suspect a successive page will have the English version of this document. Uh-huh. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, I don't know if you've seen this document before, but I wonder if you could take a couple of moments and review this document signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Meille. And you can tell us when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant, in the first paragraph of this document, first and second paragraphs, Lieutenant-Colonel Meille sets out what he characterises as very serious offence, attacks on civilian targets in the city of Sarajevo using very powerful bombs as well as heavy artillery. Now, based on your military experience, your experience with mortars, and your knowledge of the situation at the time, was the placement of ABiH, Bosnian Army, 82-millimetre mortars 500 metres behind the PTT building sufficient to attract fire of the power and calibre that General -- Colonel Meille is -- has set out in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not where those rounds landed. Perhaps I can explain. Mortars are not always the most accurate of weapons, but generally we fire more than one round and most rounds hit where they're supposed to hit. They might be short every now and then, but when they are very specific -- numerous rounds hitting in one area we cannot consider that a short. And 300 metres or 400 or 500 metres away is a different target. It's not collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So an object 300, 400 or 500 metres away, as it was in this circumstance, in your opinion, based on your experience, can't legitimately be claimed the target of the rounds that hit the PTT building and the TV building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I just clarify one question. From where the fire was supposed to have emanated, could the target, that is to say the mortar -- the Bosnian mortars, could they be seen or do they -- would they have to shoot over the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You -- they could not be seen from where they were firing, but they could be -- the firing could be observed from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then the unit designed to target it could be somewhere else. That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe I could ask one question of clarification. I mean, would this have any impact on the precision with which you would fire? If you can't see the target, would you have to measure to calculate the elevation of your mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a general rule, mortar men firing their mortars never see the target they're hitting because they're firing 2 or 3 or 4 kilometres away and they're firing from behind protected positions. Observers who -- who's task it is to find a target and give it to the mortar guns will do that and ensure that the firing is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So they could have targeted the Bosnian mortars 500 metres behind the building and missed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could have, sir, but -- and missed with one round perhaps, but not with all rounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel -- you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To refresh Your Honours' memory from yesterday, and in the context of questions that Your Honour is posing, I'd like to take this opportunity to direct your attention to one of the exhibits which my learned friend admitted to the authenticity of and was admitted into evidence today and that is P42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your indulgence one further time, Your Honour. I note that my learned friend refers to two documents in her cross-examination without tendering them into evidence, and maybe we could deal with that quickly. The numbers my case manager has provided me with are PT 00103 and PT 02364. Do I have the numbers correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's ask Ms. Isailovic whether she wishes to have these tendered as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. I would like to thank Ms. Bosnjakovic for having identified the documents. I apologise. I forgot that this should be done, so I would like these documents to be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what are their numbers? No, please give them --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not able --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please give them numbers, Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 00103 will become Exhibit D11. And 65 ter number 02364 will become Exhibit D12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, that concludes your evidence. Thanks for giving it and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my time before you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we are ready to proceed with the next witness. I would just perhaps note the time and ask Your Honour's indulgence for a few moments so that I can log out of my computer and the technology and my colleague can log in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give you a few minutes. Please call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the next witness is Milan Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would just like to take the opportunity to introduce Mr. Manoj Sachdeva, trial attorney on the team. It's his first appearance this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may proceed, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name, your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: My last name is Mandilovic, first name Milan. I was born on the 16th of June, 1949, in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about your personal background --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, Your Honours, if I could take your leave to lead the witness through these issues since I submit they are not disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, you are an ear, nose, and throat surgeon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you currently work at the State Hospital in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you qualified as a doctor in 1975. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you became an ENT specialist in 1986?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Prior to that you joined the Yugoslav national army in 1978 and you joined the medical corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you reached the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When did you reach the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you started to work at the JNA hospital in Sarajevo in 1982. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just to be clear, during the period August 1994 through to November 1995, you were the chief of the ear, nose, and throat surgery department at that hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: During that period, apart from your work in the ear, nose, and throat department, did you perform any other medical obligations or any other medical work obligations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. During the war, there is no strict division in medicine -- in medical practice; therefore, one is compelled, depending on what one is faced in the hospital, do or assist with all kinds of injuries, not only from your field of specialty. In addition to that, for the most part of the war, apart from my regular duties, I constantly visited ER and -- in our hospital --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Intensive care unit in our hospital and dressed the wounds there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you a few questions about the hospital where you worked. Just prior to the onset of the conflict, that is in April 1992, was the hospital a military or civilian hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It's a military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did that status change at any time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The status of the hospital changed on the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did it become a civilian hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it became a civilian hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what did it be come to be called?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It immediately became a State Hospital. There was a certain moment which I don't think was very important, but during the visit of President Mitterrand to Sarajevo, an idea emerged in cooperation with some humanitarian organisations that the hospital could be renamed French hospital. And in fact, in official documents, for a few months it was called that. However, thanks to humanitarian aid and connections with some other organisations, the -- it became the State Hospital and it kept that name throughout the war and after the Dayton Accords were signed and after the war itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, although the status changed to a civilian hospital, did you throughout the war continue to accept military patients?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We received all the patients that came to see us, regardless of the gender, the age, the religion, and whether they were civilians or military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I will ask you a few more questions in a few moments about the admissions, but for now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to show the witness a map, and that is 65 ter number 2738. Mr. President, I ask your indulgence when it comes up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are waiting for it to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Oh, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, do you see the map in front of you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I do, but I would be thankful it could be -- if it could be increased because it's too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm going to ask for that to be zoomed in slightly, if possible, by the court usher. Thank you. Is that the city of Sarajevo depicted there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And are you able to locate the State Hospital on that map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Here it is. How am I to point it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If you can just point at it on the monitor for now.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I ask you to take a pen or a marker and -- Doctor, I'll just give you the instruction. If you could place a circle around the hospital and to the side of the circle just mark the letters SH, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, also on that map, do you see the location of the -- the other hospital, Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you please do the same, put a circle around the hospital and mark the letters KH to the side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be numbered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P46.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps that's -- before that's done, Dr. Mandilovic can sign at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could you please sign at the bottom of the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let that be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P46.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Doctor, during the period August 1994 through to November 1995, were there any armed soldiers in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever see the ABiH, that is the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, fire mortars from the grounds of the hospital during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever see or notice any ABiH tanks or other heavy weaponry in and around the hospital complex during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I believe that it wasn't possible at all because the hospital is located in the town between two streets. So this kind of weapon could not have enough maneuverability, but that's my opinion and I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Were there any other military facilities in and around the hospital during that period, Dr. Mandilovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Military facilities, no, but within the hospital compound was, or rather, in the park around the hospital was the building that was a rehabilitation centre for members of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who typically were working inside that building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Those were mobilised doctors and nurses. They were not on the hospital staff, but were rather members, I believe, of the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were there any armed soldiers at that rehabilitation centre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any. There may have been some guard duty going on there, but not that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you in the time-period of, again, August 1994 through to November 1995, was the State Hospital the subject of sniping or shelling attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say whether it was a direct target, but in the period that you referred to, there were hits, the hospital building was hit, the main building of the hospital was hit, and it's a 12-storey building, and there were both kind of hits. Whether they were deliberate or random, it's very difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "both kind of hits," can you please explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I mean that the hospital was exposed both to artillery fire and to sniper fire at certain periods of time, but I cannot be specific. I am not an expert in that area. I would not presume to give such a decisive assessment, but the very look of the hospital clearly indicates that it had sustained a large number of destructive hits of various intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just in relation to the building itself, these destructive hits, where were they -- where were they sustained? Which part of the building were they to be seen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Literally on all 12 floors. There is not a single floor in this hospital that wasn't affected by these destructive impact of artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was there a particular side of the hospital that saw more hits than other sides?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The southern part of the building was affected much more than the other parts of the building. The southern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where did the southern part of the building face, towards which direction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The southern part I -- pardon me, overlooks Marijin Dvor - it's a large square - the Miljacka River, and across the river Miljacka it overlooks the slopes of Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to say where these hits or where these, as you said, shelling and sniping emanated from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, not only in the period that you are referring to but throughout the war, I think that the general area of the hospital and Marijin Dvor, where the hospital is located, was exposed to sniper fire from the Jewish cemetery and from Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the basis for your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis of our knowledge is that throughout the war, not only in the years that we are talking about, we constantly had wounded people coming from the location close to -- locations close to the hospital, and according to all the indicators, had been wounded by sniper hits, according to patients' statements and to the statements of those who brought them to hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, you mentioned in your previous answer to my question the areas of the Jewish cemetery and Grbavica. Please tell the Court which party to the conflict controlled those areas.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, these areas were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm not sure what time a break is taken. I'm happy to continue, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should be now, yes. We'll take the break now. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the witness here? Why isn't the witness here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, just a question of clarification from Mr. President's question to you. You told the Court that the sniper fire came from Grbavica and the Jewish cemetery according to your knowledge. What I want to ask you is: On what basis do you say that the fire, the sniper fire, came from those areas? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't make myself clear enough. A person hit by a -- by sniper fire is unable to go to the hospital on his own. Somebody must go and fetch him. That information, coupled with the location where this happened, were an indication enough for us to know where the best spots were for general movement and crossing open spaces and so on and so forth, and that's from what we were able to infer where the fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So the location you talk about where it gave you an indication where these incidents happened, why do you say that location -- from that location you could infer that the fire, as you said, came from Grbavica and the Jewish cemetery? What was particular about that location?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The point is as follows. These were two locations that were literally part of town. The separation line was the Miljacka River. Because of the proximity of the enemy line, as it were, the injuries were precise and frequent because the distances were short.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How far was Marijin Dvor from Grbavica, as the crow flies, if you can tell?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Several hundred metres as the crow flies. The Jewish cemetery was particularly close. It is on somewhat higher ground, and from the Jewish cemetery one has an excellent view of the area where Marijin Dvor is and the railway station. The Jewish cemetery is on somewhat higher ground. It is on the headland of Mount Trebevic and offers, affords, a good view of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, may I just have something clarified. This witness is not a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. This witness is not a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're examining the witness in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct. And I anticipate being another 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Doctor, you earlier talked about during the war and not just the period of August 1994 to November 1995, that all 12 floors of the building were subjected to sniping and shelling. Do you recall a particular incident in the period August to -- August 1994 through to November 1995, a particular shelling incident where you were personally involved? And if you do recall, please describe that incident to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The hospital building itself was an object of extensive destruction, of course. I have to be quite precise and I'm sure I won't be wrong if I say that the destruction of the hospital was more extensive in 1992 and 1993 than in that period; however, I was unfortunate enough to personally take part in one such event. This was in late summer of 1994. At that time there was no electricity. The elevators were not in operation, and I was taking the staircase to reach the 12th floor where my ward was. When I was at the level of the 11th floor, the entire structure was shaken. It was a clear, sunny day, but at that point everything went pitch black. As it became lighter and as I looked at my colleague who was a nurse with me there, we were all covered in soot. Our clothes were grey, and that was the closest I came in touch with danger throughout the war because I had never been closer to a shell impact than I was at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were there any injuries in that incident you describe?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I wasn't injured. An investigation was carried out afterwards. The projectile entered a room on the 11th floor and exploded there. Since the door to that room was closed and I was in the stairwell outside the corridor leading to that room, neither my colleague nor I sustained any injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I want to ask you also about sniping. Do you recall a particular incident where people in the hospital were hit by sniper fire during the period August 1994 through to November 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I do recall that as well. I wasn't on duty on that day; however, as we had 24-hour shifts, which meant that we would work for 24 hours and then rest for 24 hours, when I went to work the following day and I was touring patients, there was a -- I heard that there was a sniper incident that two patients had been hit in their extremities. I think it was in the summer of 1995. These were just slight injuries to tissue, and it all ended well, but nevertheless it happened. To make matters quite clear, I have to tell you that this did not take place in the central building of the hospital, the 12th-storey building, but in an annex to the west toward the railway station, which was some four storeys high, and I believe that the incident took place on the third floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're wondering whether the Prosecutor could tell us the following when Mr. Mandilovic was referring to this first incident, what was the date of that incident and I wasn't able to infer from the documents because we have 34 of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't exactly recall the date. Do you mean when I experienced the direct impact?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you the date. I only know that it was in late summer -- at any rate, summer of 1994. I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I think that's what the witness initially said, Mr. President, late summer 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Doctor, in addition to your observations, being a doctor in the hospital, but also as a citizen of Sarajevo, how would you describe the shelling and sniping in the city of Sarajevo between the periods August 1994 through to November 1995? Very briefly, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I said something to that effect already. The fact is that 1994 and 1995 were, in view of the citizens of Sarajevo, somewhat easier; and if you allow me, I can explain that in a couple of sentences. The intensity of fighting was somewhat less, probably thanks to politics. The Blue Routes were partially opened, which were used to bring food and medical supplies to Sarajevo. Of course, they were open only partially and the -- these periods were short-lived. They would be closed soon thereafter. There was several attempts to fix the power supply at last, although this was also short-lived. However, generally speaking, the situation was somewhat better. On the other hand, we were already in the third year of the war and the population was exhausted, both psychologically and physically. They were experiencing all the effects that such a situation entails. It is very difficult to live through such a long time-period in a town under siege without the basic necessities of life with the separation lines running so close.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Doctor, if I could just ask you. You said that the -- there was several attempts to fix the power supply. I want to ask you: Why did the power supply need to be fixed? Why was it broken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I don't know. But the fact of the matter is that as of May or June - it's difficult for me to pin-point the time - of 1992, Sarajevo did not have electricity. I can't tell you that we did not have electricity all the time, but generally speaking, there was none to be had in the town, in the hospital. Throughout that time, we were able to work thanks to the generators that we had and that we used sparingly and rationally. I'm speaking as a civilian now, not as a member of the hospital staff. We were looking forward to having regular electricity; however, from day-to-day we would have it sporadically because it would soon be cut off because someone had done something to it and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in the period, again August 1994 through to November 1995, can you say something about the frequency of patients or admissions in your hospital with shelling and sniping injuries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of what I said just a while ago, and I do still abide by that, that the intensity of fighting was somewhat less in that period, still there was a war on and tensions were escalating. I personally have two events firmly etched in my mind because they marked the onset of terrible, complete destruction. This was the 16th of June, 1995, and I remember this date because of this other thing, and which is simply that it's my birthday. On that date, the army -- the BH army started an attempt to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. The following day is also fresh in my memory, which is the day of the Markale massacre, which took place at the end of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I will ask you questions about those two incidents you speak about in a moment, but I just want to get back to the general situation. Let me put it this way: Did you -- did your hospital receive patients on a weekly basis or on a daily basis or on a monthly basis that showed shelling and sniping injuries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Our hospital was open 24 hours a day. As I said at the start of my testimony, our hospital admitted everyone. I can tell you that not a week passed by without there having been persons brought in, either due to sniping or shelling. They were brought in from different locations because only three hospitals in the town provided surgical care. Depending on the locality where the event would happen, the patients would be taken to one of these hospitals. I repeat, we would constantly admit persons. There wasn't a week that went by without there having been patients coming in. Of course, the numbers of persons coming in varied. It is difficult to tell you the precise number, but you have the hospital records which give an accurate reflection of the numbers of patients brought in and the times of their admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The persons that were brought in, as you say, on a weekly basis, could you give us an estimate of the ratio between the military -- because you said that you still continued to receive military patients, but the ratio between military personnel and civilians being brought into the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that throughout the war, including the period we're discussing right now, the approximate ratio was 80:20 per cent in favour of civilians. In other words, the number of injured civilians was always vastly greater than the number of military personnel admitted into our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How did you establish these people were civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: One of the significant elements involved in the admission of patients was their personal background and their personal data, names, age, place of birth, and so on, and it was on the basis of this that we would admit them. Also what was taken into account was the way the patients were brought into the hospital, whether it was by way of a vehicle belonging to an organisation or institution or whether they were brought in by people, passers-by, their friends or members of their family. In addition to that, military personnel would have military IDs on them, they would be uniformed; and on the basis of that, we could easily establish whether a person was a civilian or military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, among the 80 per cent or so of the civilians that were brought into your hospital, what types of injuries did you and your colleagues observe when they were brought in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Look, it is difficult to give you a precise answer now. When it comes to Sarajevo, there were two types of injuries: Injuries caused by shell shrapnel and injuries caused by gun-fire. The difference is easily visible because the tissue damaged by a shell is vastly damaged. You have lesions, you have bone fractures, injuries inflicted on extremities, whereas gun-fire injuries show the -- the point where bullets entered and exited and so on and so forth, and they are by far less severe, which does not mean that gun-fire injuries are less dangerous. The point at matter is which part of body was hit by shrapnel or by a bullet, but I repeat, the difference is easy to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Earlier on you mentioned the market massacre in August 1995. Do you recall the date that the -- the precise date of that incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 28th of August, 1995, in the morning hours. I was on duty that day. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And please describe to the Court what was the situation like in your hospital on that day, very briefly if you can.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the morning that all of a sudden - and there had been silence in the town - a strong detonation could be heard and one could not assess the distance. Sometime later, cars started flowing in, privately-owned cars, ambulances, bringing in large numbers of seriously wounded persons, and I say "seriously wounded," because one could immediately observe that the injuries were caused by shell shrapnel. These were gashing lacerations on different parts of bodies, depending on where the person had been hit. At that point in time, as the vehicles were pouring in, bringing the wounded, we were overcrowding down there in the emergency ward. We resorted to the principles of wartime surgery, and these are principles governing situations where you have to deal with large numbers of wounded people in a very short period of time. We conducted triage, which meant that we examined the injured person, assessed his or her health condition, which was to tell us how urgent the treatment of that particular wounded is. What does this mean? This means that you have to first treat those who are critically wounded, whose life was in danger, and to go on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just three brief questions from your answer, if I may. Firstly, how far as the crow flies was your hospital from -- from where the marketplace was, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a thousand metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you mentioned that persons were brought in. Were these persons military or civilian or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Again, most of them were civilians this time as well. I do recall seeing a military person here and there, but their numbers were negligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How many persons, again roughly, were admitted to your hospital on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, at that point some 40 persons arrived at the hospital. Of course not all of them were wounded equally or had the same type of wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I want to ask you some more general questions about life in Sarajevo. Firstly, with respect to public transport. Did you ever take the tram during the period August 1994 through to November 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No. The tram wasn't running in 1994. I believe it started running when -- at the time the Dayton negotiations started, which was in late 1995. I can't give you the exact date. I didn't take the tram because as a matter of fact I didn't need to. I would go to work and back from work on a military bus. We were lucky enough to have organised transport.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: On medical staff bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: During that period, however, were people taking trams on -- occasionally or frequently?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm speaking as a civilian. I wondered how people weren't afraid to take the tram that was running from the west to the east across Marijin Dvor. The fact of the matter is - and I'm sure this can be found in documents somewhere - there had been some incidents involving trams and some people were seriously wounded while riding on trams. I know that there were several such instances, but despite them, trams continued running.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "some incidents," what do you mean? Which type of incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there was sniper fire or some other sort of fire upon trams. There were people wounded, and I recall seeing them at our hospital because I remember people saying that they were injured while on trams. This was in late 1995. There was constant media coverage of such incidents, and I recall seeing destroyed trams with bloodstains all over the seats and so on and so forth. So I do remember such incidents, and I never rode on trams.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the sniping in the city, were you aware of any measures that were taken by the people of Sarajevo to protect themselves from sniping?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as the war went on, the services taking care of the population in general, such as the civilian protection, tried to prevent sniping. At crossroads that were open to the locations that we mentioned a while ago, they would place large concrete barricades, containers in two or three rows in order to prevent such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Doctor, my last -- my penultimate question I should say. Were you -- during the period of the war, and in particular through 1994 and into 1995, were you ever prevented from leaving the city by the Bosnian government authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't find myself in such a situation because I didn't ask to leave the town. But realistically speaking, I don't think I would have been able to leave. There was a war on, and persons with high qualifications, specialists, are not allowed to leave that easily. I mean, I'm just speaking hypothetically now, but I didn't ask to leave in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I want to talk to you about hospital records. Firstly, during your time at the State Hospital, did you come across records that were issued by the hospital? Did you yourself issue records, medical documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Despite the difficult situation, in all aspects that I spoke about earlier, we were aware that records were a very important element in medical field and otherwise. Therefore, each department had their own protocol, each ward in the hospital, then the admission ward also had their own records. So based on these protocols and records, one can practically see when each patient was examined; what doctor's orders, instructions, were; who was admitted to the hospital; how long they stayed in the hospital; et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with respect to hospital -- medical records from the Kosevo Hospital, did you ever have occasion to see such records?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, very often -- I don't mean their actual hospital books and records, but I did see on many occasions their medical reports and findings by their physicians. Why was that? And I would like to clarify this. The reason was because that the Kosevo Hospital and our hospital were the only real hospital in town at the time that offered all kinds of medical treatment to the sick and the injured, and there was an ongoing cooperation between our two institutions. And very frequently a patient, or rather, an injured person would be examined and given medical assistance in one hospital and would subsequently go for later checks -- check-ups in another hospital for a variety of reasons, whether he was unable to come to the original hospital, the other one was closer to his place of residence, there was shelling, et cetera. So as I said, throughout the war we had very good cooperation and good understanding and we were even close to one another physically. And we helped each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, at this stage I intend to offer into evidence a series of medical records from both those institutions, the State and the Kosevo Hospitals. Now, in the interests of time, there are about 70 to 100 pages, each representing a separate medical record, which were shown to the witness in proofing and an affidavit, so to speak, has been obtained containing the lists of those records. And I would like to show that affidavit to the witness and ask him a few questions about those records, the pages contained in the list. The other alternative is to go through each document on the e-court one by one, and the Prosecution's submission is that clearly that would take time and it's more efficient to -- for the court registrar to indicate a number later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, let me hear your views on this method of admitting these documents. Are you contesting this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at that moment I had a very important concentration before I started my cross-examinations and we are nearing to tracing some documents at the last moment, virtually in the last seconds, and due to the importance of this document, I really didn't hear what was being discussed here and I do apologise if I've -- if it is possible that I'm being told again what the matter is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat the method that you're proposing, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. What I would like to say first is that the Defence and I also indicated to the Legal Officer the documents that I have shown the witness in proofing and the exact pages have been communicated to the Defence 72 hours before the witness was set to testify, as was required by Mr. President and Your Honours. And the suggestion is that rather than go through each document one by one on the e-court, is to simply ask the witness whether he stands by his affidavit here under oath and for those pages to be given an exhibit number by the court officer, in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of the affidavit, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honours. And that was precisely in front of us in the last few minutes, and at the very last moment we detected a few things that the Prosecution failed to put on e-court and it doesn't exist there in relation to the investigation that was conducted on the 8th of November, 1994. And it probably overlaps with this date. And we have uncovered a precious document for Defence a few seconds ago and we sent a mail to the Prosecution, telling them that we have no choice but to have these two documents tendered and used here, but they were not either in the investigation mentioned here because that was an UNPROFOR investigation, and I think that this document was not presented to the witness, whereas it shows a lot, this document I mean. I'm not insisting on this, Your Honours, that everything has to be read from A to Z, but since we dealt with this, we managed somehow at the very last moment to discover these two documents. I'm not trying to compel anyone to do things that are unnecessary. However, in this particular instance, I think this will be very useful for the Defence and after what we heard the witness saying, we tried to search the e-court and we found some things and we can definitely say that this document is not on e-court. I do apologise to the Prosecution, but it doesn't exist either in the documents presented to the witness relating to this criminal investigation described under item --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that the document is not accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not -- excuse me, can I have a short consultation, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, let me just ask Mr. Sachdeva, what are you hoping to establish by this document, by these records?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you're asking the relevance here of the medical records, the Prosecution submits that they pertain to two scheduled incidents appended to the amended indictment and they are records of what we submit to be people that were injured in those incidents. Perhaps, if I could just enlighten my learned friend, what I'm proposing to do is to -- the document I'm speaking about is a spreadsheet, so to speak, a Microsoft Word spreadsheet containing a list of records that the witness has been shown. It is not a criminal investigation from the 8th of August, 1994, and it is not something on the exhibit list. It's simply a mechanism used to efficiently tender material that would otherwise take over an hour, I would submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, if we are talking about the documents relating to injuries, I never had any doubt about medical records of any physician for all these years in this Tribunal. Of course, if this pertains to medical records, I'm not going to dispute that. And in that respect we have a very clear position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's really just a shorthand way of getting the evidence in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, then put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Doctor, can you please turn to the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. My signature and the date. Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you please confirm to the Court by looking through the pages that the records -- the pages indicated on that document are records that you have seen and confirmed the validity -- confirmed that they are copies of valid medical records from Kosevo and State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Both from the Kosevo Hospital and from the State Hospital, yes, I confirm that and I stand by that firmly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to offer the documents contained in that spreadsheet into evidence, and the Prosecution submits that the easiest way to identify the records would be to assign a P -- an exhibit number to each and every page; in other words, the page as identified by a separate ERN number, if it pleases you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we just examine one as an example? If you look at number 14, just take --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- random number 14, the description is: "Eye department, Kosevo Hospital, admission record." With what -- what would that indicate, if I ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This record shows the following: The full name of the patient, the diagnosis, and the findings referring to the patient to be hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The only question that I have is whether even acknowledging that it is a spreadsheet in the description section, whether it wouldn't have been more helpful to have -- if we take number 14, what the injury was, you know. What was the nature of the injury sustained, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- the Prosecution would be happy to do that. I would just add that what the witness is doing is simply validating that these are credible records from his institution, and not necessarily speaking to the contents. And we will be -- the Prosecution will be bringing witnesses, live witnesses, 92 ter witnesses, some of whom are victims -- who are victims, we allege, of these incidents and would speak to the individual records. In addition, you would have, as we've heard today, overview evidence about the people who were injured in these incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will be bringing witnesses from the scheduled incidents and unscheduled who will speak to these injuries?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Of course I can't say that they would speak to every single record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: However they will speak, for example, if they were injured to the cause of their injuries. What the witness is simply doing is saying that they are valid records that he has seen in the course of his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see no objection to admitting it. The Chamber will admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was your proposal, Mr. Sachdeva, that each page be given a separate exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that couldn't be done now. The registry will do that overnight. And you take that approach -- why do you take that approach? Is it because later on we may have to refer to these records?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Absolutely. Also, they will be part of argument in terms of the casualties we allege were caused by these incidents. And I would also add that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I meant was why number them individually, as distinct from globally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Because the records aren't all the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. The registry will do this exercise overnight because there are too many to be tackled at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I would just like to show the witness a still from a video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that will be the end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. This is the main building of the State Hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Which side of that building is shown on that still?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: This is the southern side facing Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you see damage on that side of the building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see. Of course I can. Every storey has some kind of damage. If I may observe the following: This is not the picture taken at the end of the war because the damage was much more extensive at the end of the war. If you look carefully at this picture, you can see that there were a few intact windows, the window-panes are intact and not broken, but if you look at this building towards the end of 1995 there was not a single glass that was not broken on the hospital. This was my personal observation because I kept looking at it all the time and I'm telling you this from my own memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to offer that into evidence, that still, if it can be -- if it can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P47.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that's the examination-in-chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have five minutes, please begin the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will try to concentrate at least to one thing, and let it be, Your Honours, the possibility for asking once again, or rather, putting map number 6 in front of the witness. [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] But before that, I have to explain something to you, Your Honours. Witness Mandilovic gave two statements. One he gave on the 11th of February, 2000, at the time when -- actually referring to the time and the events encompassed by the responsibility of Mr. Galic. The second statement was given a few days ago on the 5th of January, 2007, in English, through videolink if I understood correctly, or by phone, and this statement was recorded in English. I don't know how much is Mr. Mandilovic capable or how much -- or what his command of English language and does he speak English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave my statement in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like an explanation from the Prosecution because what he received is his statement in English, and only after that, on last Friday, we received the translation. Unfortunately, that was my -- our mistake. Perhaps we didn't have time to give it to the accused; however, this is irrelevant. We are not objecting to this at this point in time. The only thing we would like to hear is to get an explanation under which circumstances this statement was given, if the OTP can provide us with this explanation, because the statement was given over the phone in English and the witness doesn't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd be glad to assist. Firstly, the statement was not given over the phone, it was not taken over the phone; it was done, as you said, on video, videolink. It was done with an investigator and an interpreter in The Hague with the witness in the Sarajevo field office of the United Nations with another investigator and with another interpreter. There was, as we say, simultaneous interpretation as the questions are being asked and answered and this is how statements are done in the OTP. They are typically drawn up in English after the witness has been given an opportunity to review it with an interpreter by his or her side, and this was duly done in this situation. We immediately disclosed, because the Prosecution knew the witness was supposed to come relatively earlier, we immediately disclosed the English version and we sent it off to the CLSS unit for an official translation. And as soon as that was completed, we disclosed it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The translated version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I may just confer with my case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That was on the 10th of January this year, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandilovic, we have just a few minutes left before adjournment. Can we just look again where the hospital was situated. Can you show us, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: This image here is blurred; it's a very bad image. It is impossible to identify anything, not only the hospital, in this map that you gave me. There's just a cluster of black squares signifying facilities, and I cannot identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just do it approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then you spoke about the hospital being mostly threatened from Grbavica, and we all know here where Grbavica is, but can you please show us where the Jewish cemetery is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It's just across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us where it is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So it is exactly under Debelo Brdo where the Muslim forces were. Do you know that the Muslim forces were on Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that. Am I right to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, and possibly this is a little bit too late, but the witness has just said it is virtually impossible for him to identify anything on this map, not only the hospital, so I wonder the value of continuing with this line of questioning where he is asked to mark particular areas and locations on this map. Perhaps my learned friend could show Mr. Mandilovic the map that the Prosecution showed him in chief. It might be easier for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that he asked is: It is exactly on Debelo Brdo where the Muslim forces were. Do you know that the Muslim forces were on Debelo Brdo? Well, I mean, the answer to that doesn't appear to me to require the witness showing anything on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. I was referring to the previous two questions, and I realise I rose a little bit late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let the witness answer and then we'll have to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just received the answer, and since the witness doesn't know I wasn't insisting so much and Mr. Sachdeva is right. I didn't insist on whether the Muslim forces were there. This is going to be proven in some other testimonies. I'm only asking whether Debelo Brdo, the elevation of Debelo Brdo and in the way he showed us indicates that the Jewish cemetery was very close to the bottom of Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is below Debelo Brdo, but I don't know who held Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. How close was it. Have you ever been to Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even though you are from Sarajevo?
